Micromeshes: clusters, cuts and the GPU draw

Reference Engine Last updated: 2026-11-21 Source: micromeshes.md

A mesh is cut into clusters of at most 128 triangles and a hierarchy of simplified levels. Each frame a compute pass picks the coarsest cut whose error is invisible and one draw renders it, now through the lit scene renderer and its G-buffer. This page shows what exists, with renders from the real GPU path, and what is still missing.

Micromeshes are our own design (see graphics-roadmap.md for the plan and the review of the original proposal). Everything on this page is implemented and tested except the items under What is missing.

1. What you are looking at#

2. In the scene: the lit G-buffer draw#

Turn on Micromesh in a Mesh Renderer (the Inspector shows it with its Micromesh error (px); scripts and scenes see the same two fields) and the scene renderer draws that mesh as a cluster cut instead of a plain mesh: same lit shader (scene_lit.frag), same G-buffer, so Photon, SSAO and TAA need nothing new.

Piece What it does
MeshRendererComponent::micromesh, micromeshPixels the switch and the error budget in screen pixels (converted to world units per metre with the camera's projection and the view height)
GpuSceneRenderer::micromeshAssetFor once per mesh asset and geometry revision: welds the vertices that agree on position, normal and UV (meshes are often stored unindexed), builds the hierarchy with the mesh's own normals, UVs and tangents, uploads it
beginMicromeshFrame once per frame, when the draws are final: groups the entities by mesh asset (every entity of a mesh is one instance of it), uploads one matrix buffer per asset and resets the index arena
cullMicromeshView compute, outside any render pass: one dispatch chain per asset and view (the camera first, then each sun cascade) cuts every instance of the mesh at once
micromesh_compact.comp the same cut, frustum and back-face tests as the per-cluster pass, in four passes (reset, count, reserve, copy): every selected cluster appends its indices to a shared index arena, so each instance is one indexed draw and memory follows what is visible
scene_micromesh.vert, shadow_micromesh.vert the scene vertex shader (positions, normals, UVs, tangents and vertex colours in five slots, normals by the inverse transpose) and the positions-only cascade shader; both read the matrix from the instance buffer
caffeine_session_micromesh_stats (C ABI v14) draws, selected clusters, selected and source triangles of the last frame (blocking read-back, for tools and tests); CaffeineRenderStats::micromesh_draws is the cheap counter

Details worth knowing:

  • Shadows. The sun's cascades cut the mesh too: the same hierarchy with an error budget of four shadow texels (a world distance, since a cascade is orthographic, with no back-face test and a frustum test per cascade), drawn by shadow_micromesh.vert into the same shadow atlas. Same hierarchy means no cracks; a coarser cut means far fewer triangles in the shadow pass. Point and spot shadows still draw the full mesh. The editor viewport renders without shadow maps by default (a deliberate editor cost choice); ViewportSettings::shadows (C ABI v14, CaffeineViewportSettings::shadows) turns them on, which is how the images and tests here are made.
  • The arena. One index buffer serves every mesh and view of a frame, so memory follows what is visible, not what exists: this scene asks for 1.8 to 8.2 million indices a frame over its 6 views (the camera and 5 cascades) and the arena settled at 32 MB for 81 rocks, where one full-size index buffer per rock would be 80 MB and grows with the rock count. It starts at 16 MB and grows by itself (doubling, up to 256 MB) when a counter read-back every 15 frames shows it was too small; a cut that does not fit is not drawn that frame (overflowed in the stats), so growth shows as a few frames of missing shadows or rocks, never as a corrupt draw. The camera is cut first, so it is the last to lose.
  • Sub-meshes, scale, colours. A mesh with several materials gets one hierarchy per sub-mesh, drawn with its material. An OBJ's usemtl groups are sub-meshes, and the Mesh Filter's Material slots (a.mat;b.mat) give each an authored material: the renderer then makes one draw per slot, so a slot can be alpha-tested or have wind (it draws plain) while the others stay Micromeshes. A non-uniform scale is handled: errors and bounds use the largest scale (conservative) and the back-face test is skipped for such an instance. Vertex colours are carried through the build (averaged at a collapse). This also fixed the plain scene shaders, which transformed normals by the model matrix and shaded a stretched mesh wrongly (now the inverse transpose).
  • A multi-draw of clusters is not free on the CPU. SDL3 GPU has no indirect-count draw, so the per-cluster path (one indirect draw per cluster, used by the instanced field below) costs encoding time that grows with the cluster count. The scene path compacts instead: one draw per instance whatever the cut selects. A test checks the compacted cut keeps exactly the same clusters and triangles as the per-cluster one.
  • Dense meshes without materials were slow to draw at all. For a mesh with no material or sibling PNG, resolveMeshAlbedo re-read and scanned the whole mesh file for texture names on every draw of every frame (4 to 8 ms of CPU per draw). It is now remembered until the file's modification time changes (this speeds up any such mesh, Micromesh or not).
  • A renderer limit found on the way: the pipeline description kept only 4 vertex buffers; a fifth was dropped silently (the vertex colours read as black). It is 8 now.

Occlusion#

An instance can also be culled against what last frame's depth buffer shows: Mesh Renderer -> Micromesh occlusion. Each frame the previous depth buffer is reduced to a farthest-depth pyramid (MicromeshHzb, micromesh_hzb.comp: one storage buffer, level after level, each texel the maximum of the four below it; Photon's Min-Z pyramid keeps the nearest depth, the opposite reduction). The camera's compacting cull then projects each cluster's bounding sphere with last frame's matrices, picks the pyramid level where its footprint spans at most two texels, and drops the cluster when the sphere's nearest depth is beyond the farthest depth of every texel under it. Anything undecidable stays visible: a sphere near or behind the camera, one that reaches past the screen edge.

This is a single-phase test, not the two-phase one of the roadmap. It uses last frame's picture, so a cluster that was hidden last frame and becomes visible this frame (the camera moved, or an occluder moved away) shows one frame late. In the swing above that costs a few edge pixels: the worst single pixel of a frame differs by up to 250 / 255 (a rock's edge arriving one frame late), while the mean difference never exceeds 0.15 / 255. That is why the switch is off by default and per instance. A true two-phase test (draw the clusters seen last frame, rebuild the pyramid from that depth, test the rest) needs the opaque pass split in two, and is not done. Only the camera's cut is tested; shadow cascades are not (their view is the light's). Needs a previous frame of the same view at the same size, so the first frame after a resize culls nothing; the pyramid costs a depth read and about 1.3x the depth buffer in memory.

Benchmark#

./scripts/render-micromesh-scene-docs.sh also prints this table (a fixed scene: 81 rocks of 81 408 triangles, a 72-frame flight, camera cut at 1.5 px, cascades at four texels, then the same flight with plain instanced meshes). Triangle counts are exact and reproducible; the times are CPU encoding time (SDL3 GPU has no portable GPU timestamps), so they say nothing about GPU cost.

Benchmark set#

./scripts/benchmark-micromesh.sh runs the reproducible benchmark set: a dense rock field, a forest of dense trees and a terrain, each flown by a fixed 40-frame camera path at 640x360 with the sun's shadows on, through every renderer path that applies. The content is generated in code from hashes (no assets; a test checks the OBJ files are byte-identical between runs and their triangle counts fixed), so the triangle and draw counts are exactly the same on every run (two runs here matched to the last digit). The times are not: wall is a whole frame including the read-back of the picture, so it follows the GPU but also the machine (two runs here agreed within about 5%): compare rows of one run, not numbers between machines. Encode is CPU command-recording time. BENCH_OUT=<dir> keeps the raw per-frame numbers (benchmarks.json).

Rock field: 81 rocks x 81 408 triangles (6.6 M), a low flight.

configuration triangles (min / median / max) draw calls wall ms encode ms
plain meshes (instanced) 1 139 714 / 3 215 618 / 5 861 378 2 / 2 / 2 15.1 / 23.8 / 40.8 4.3 / 5.2 / 12.0
Micromesh 177 992 / 527 412 / 833 391 15 / 40 / 73 8.9 / 13.3 / 19.5 5.9 / 8.6 / 13.8

6.1x fewer triangles, median wall time 0.56 of the plain's.

Forest: 300 trees x 47 808 triangles (a barky trunk and three lumpy crowns, brown and green vertex colours; 14.3 M), a flight between them.

configuration triangles (min / median / max) draw calls wall ms encode ms
plain meshes (instanced) 908 354 / 5 139 362 / 10 756 802 2 / 2 / 2 24.4 / 49.4 / 93.5 14.8 / 15.5 / 28.1
Micromesh 313 828 / 1 570 378 / 2 864 164 20 / 108 / 226 23.1 / 37.3 / 58.0 18.2 / 26.9 / 39.5

3.3x fewer triangles, median wall time 0.75 of the plain's, but the CPU pays: median encoding goes from 15.5 to 26.9 ms because every tree is its own draw (108 against the two instanced batches). The forest here is opaque; leaf cards with alpha stay on the instanced path by design, so a real forest is a mix and this one is the best case for Micromesh.

Terrain: an 800 m terrain at two grid sizes, a flight over it. The engine's chunked terrain path only (Micromesh does not draw terrain yet).

grid source triangles triangles submitted (min / median / max) draw calls wall ms encode ms
513 x 513 524 288 192 512 / 227 328 / 313 344 94 / 111 / 153 11.2 / 15.5 / 29.2 6.1 / 9.6 / 22.1
1025 x 1025 2 097 152 724 992 / 839 680 / 1 173 504 354 / 410 / 573 21.3 / 32.5 / 38.7 12.9 / 22.6 / 28.0

The terrain's chunk LOD already submits 43 % (513) and 40 % (1025) of the source triangles, one draw per visible chunk. Four times the triangles cost about twice the frame time. (Writing this benchmark showed that terrain draws were missing from the frame counters, which reported 0 triangles and 0 draws for a terrain; they count now.) This is the baseline a terrain cluster path has to beat.

The viewport HUD shows the same counters live: ... · 610.3k tris · 74 draws · 72 micromesh (triangles submitted, draws, and how many meshes were drawn as a cut).

What it does not do yet: skinned meshes (their vertices move every frame, so rest-pose clusters would be wrong: they draw plain, by design), alpha-tested or translucent materials and wind-animated foliage (they stay on the instanced path, by design: the roadmap keeps foliage there), and point and spot shadows (full mesh). Each instance is still its own draw (instances of one mesh share geometry, the dispatch and the arena, not a draw: that would need vertex pulling). The hierarchy is built the first time a mesh is seen, about a second for 80 000 triangles; an offline .micromesh section in the .caf is the planned way to not pay it at run time.

3. Instances in one dispatch: a field of rocks#

One hierarchy can be drawn many times. Each instance has an affine transform with a uniform scale, and the cull pass decides per instance: its own cut (error and distance), its own frustum test and its own back-face test. The whole field is one compute dispatch and one drawIndexedIndirect.

Item Where
MicromeshGpu::setInstances(transforms) uploads four vec4 per instance (the first three matrix rows, then the scale) as a compute buffer and as a graphics storage buffer
Cull index invocation g = instance * clusterCount + cluster; spheres, errors and the cone axis are brought to world space before the tests
Draw argument firstInstance = g; the vertex shader reads instance = g / clusterCount, cluster = g % clusterCount and the matrix from instanceBuffer()
readStats() visible clusters and triangles over every instance (blocking read-back, for tools and tests)

A far instance is cut coarser than a near one even when it is bigger, and an instance behind the camera or far to the side contributes no draw at all.

4. Shading normals#

A cut is only useful if it shades like the exact mesh. The build now carries a unit shading normal per vertex: smooth, angle-weighted normals for the source vertices, and for every vertex a collapse creates, the normalised sum of the two it replaced. The normals are part of the bytes (.micromesh version 2) and MicromeshGpu::drawLit binds them as a second vertex buffer (slot 1, Float3).

What it does not do: the normals are averaged, so detail below the cut is smoothed away (the rightmost image has lost the small bumps). A normal map on the lit pipeline is what puts it back; carrying UVs through the collapses is the next attribute.

5. Texture coordinates#

build(positions, indices, uvs) also carries texture coordinates. A vertex a collapse creates takes the UV of the closest point of the edge it replaced. UV seams are never simplified across: a seam is a boundary of split vertices (an edge used by one triangle), and the build already locks every boundary at every level, so both ends of a collapsed edge always lie on the same UV island. MicromeshGpu::drawTextured binds the UVs as a third vertex buffer (slot 2, Float2).

The price of locked seams: a mesh with many UV islands simplifies less. This rock has one seam and still stops at about 11 000 of 82 000 triangles in this view; an atlas with dozens of islands will stop sooner. Measure on your meshes.

6. How it works#

Stage Where What happens
Cluster micromesh/Micromesh.cpp triangles sorted along a Morton curve, split into clusters of at most 128 triangles and 128 vertices; each gets a bounding sphere, a back-face cone and a local vertex remap
Hierarchy same clusters are grouped (4 at a time), each group is merged, simplified by quadric edge collapse with its boundary locked, and split again, up to one root
Error same the error of a group is the larger of its collapse error (an RMS distance, in world units) and its children's, plus an epsilon: strictly monotonic, with a sphere that contains the children's
Cut selectCut, micromesh_cull.comp a cluster is drawn when its own error is within the budget and its parent's is not (optionally divided by the distance to its sphere, a projected error)
Cull micromesh_cull.comp the same pass tests the frustum and the back-face cone, and writes one indexed-draw argument set per cluster, with indexCount 0 when culled
Draw render/MicromeshGpu one drawIndexedIndirect(args, 0, clusterCount): the same call every frame, nothing read back, no atomics

Because a group's boundary is locked at every level, and a cluster and its parent are never both selected, any cut tiles the surface without cracks. This is tested, not assumed: every cut of a sphere and a torus is a closed manifold (each edge in exactly two triangles) at twelve thresholds.

7. Using it#

text
C ABI v12   caffeine_micromesh_build(positions, indices, &stats, &bytes, &size)   -> versioned .micromesh bytes
C ABI v14   caffeine_session_micromesh_stats(session, &stats)   -> draws, clusters, triangles, source triangles, views,
                                                                   arena use and capacity, cuts that did not fit
            CaffeineRenderStats::micromesh_draws, CaffeineViewportSettings::shadows, stats.occlusion
Inspector   Mesh Renderer -> Micromesh, Micromesh error (px), Micromesh occlusion; the viewport HUD shows tris, draws and micromesh draws
Rust        Engine::micromesh_build(&positions, &indices) -> MicromeshBake { bytes, clusters, levels, root_clusters, max_error, ... }
C++ core    Micromesh::build(positions, indices, {normals, uvs, tangents, colors}) / selectCut / serialize / deserialize
            Render::MicromeshGpu::upload, then either the per-cluster path (setInstances / cull / draw* / readStats)
            or the scene path (setSceneInstances / cullScene / drawSceneSlot / readSceneView) with a MicromeshArena
            and, for occlusion, a MicromeshHzb built from the previous depth (MicromeshCullParams::occlusion)

The build is offline work (a bake): it is deterministic, so the same mesh gives byte-identical output, and it takes under a second for a 20 000-triangle mesh. Never call it per frame.

The agent query render_stats (and Engine::render_stats(), C ABI v13) reports what a frame drew: meshes, culled by the frustum, draw calls, instanced draw calls, triangles and CPU pass times.

Regenerate the images and GIFs of sections 1, 3, 4 and 5 with ./scripts/render-micromesh-docs.sh (hidden tests with the tags [.micromesh-docs], [.micromesh-field], [.micromesh-normals] and [.micromesh-uv] render the frames on the GPU; scripts/compose_micromesh_docs.py composes them), and section 2's with ./scripts/render-micromesh-scene-docs.sh (an env-gated Doppio engine test through the real scene renderer, plus the benchmark table).

8. What the tests prove#

  • On the CPU (tests/test_micromesh.cpp): clusters respect the limits, every level is coarser, a closed mesh ends in one root, errors only grow toward the root and spheres contain their children's, cuts are crack-free, view-dependent cuts are coarser far away, an open mesh keeps its boundary and terminates, back-face cones never hide a facing cluster, rebuilds are byte-identical, truncated bytes are refused.
  • On the GPU (tests/test_micromesh_gpu.cpp, tests/test_rhi_indirect.cpp): the cut the compute pass selects equals the CPU's at four distances and three budgets, the cone filter equals isBackFacing, the frustum test equals the same sphere-plane test on the CPU, indirect arguments decide what is drawn, and a compute pass can write them.
  • Scene path: the Doppio engine test micromesh_draw_matches_the_plain_mesh_and_submits_fewer_triangles renders a dense OBJ rock on a floor under the sun, with shadow maps on, through the real renderer both ways: the picture (shadow included) stays within a few / 255 of the plain mesh's, the cut keeps about a third of the triangles close up, the camera and at least one cascade were cut into one arena with nothing overflowing, micromesh_draws is 1 with the switch on and 0 after switching it off, and the HUD label says so. micromesh_handles_non_uniform_scale_submeshes_and_vertex_colours does the same for a stretched rock, a rock with two materials and a rock with a vertex colour. [compact] (GPU) checks that the arena's compacted cut keeps exactly the clusters and triangles of the per-cluster cut for instances of several scales (one non-uniform), at three cameras and four budgets, for a view that is not the first (slot offsets), that the arena holds exactly the cut, and that a cut which does not fit is not drawn and is reported. [colors] checks vertex colours survive every level and the bytes.
  • Normals ([normals]): every vertex normal is a unit vector at every level and follows the surface (on a sphere, within 26 degrees of the radial direction at all 16 levels, including the coarsest), the normals round-trip through the bytes, and on the GPU a coarse cut lit with carried normals is within 6/255 of the exact render while facet normals are more than twice as far.
  • UVs ([uv]): on a torus with real seams, every UV stays in range, every vertex of every level sits where its UV says to within a small multiple of its level's simplification error, no triangle of any cut spans a seam (the widest UV jump inside a triangle stays under half the texture), and the UVs round-trip through the bytes. The rock render test checks that the bump map and the checker stay close to the exact render at three cuts.
  • Occlusion ([occlusion], GPU): a wall rendered into a depth buffer, its pyramid built (the corner texel is the sky's 1.0, the middle the wall's depth, the top level keeps the farthest), then three instances of the sphere: the one behind the wall is culled, the one beside it and the one in front stay. In the Doppio engine, micromesh_occlusion_hides_what_last_frames_depth_shows_behind_a_wall puts six rocks on each side of a wall: the camera's cut drops to between a quarter and three quarters of the open one, the cut was tested (occlusion in the stats), and the picture stays within 1.5 / 255.
  • Instances ([instances]): with four transforms (scales 0.5 to 2, rotations, distances up to 70 m) every instance's GPU cut equals the CPU cut of the same mesh seen from the camera in that instance's space, at three error budgets; a far instance is cut coarser than a near one; instances behind the camera or beside the frustum draw nothing; the cone test equals isBackFacing in each instance's own space, including one turned half a turn; and one indirect draw puts two instances where their matrices say (two mirror-image discs with an empty gap).

9. What is missing#

Not done yet (also in the roadmap)
  • Point and spot shadows. Only the sun's cascades cut; point and spot shadow maps draw the full mesh.
  • One draw per instance. Batching the instances of a mesh into a single draw needs vertex pulling (the matrix chosen per index range); today they share geometry, the dispatch and the arena but not a draw.
  • By design. Skinned meshes, alpha-tested or translucent materials and wind foliage draw as plain meshes or stay instanced.
  • Non-uniform scale in the per-cluster path. The scene path handles it; the per-cluster path (the instanced field) still assumes one scale.
  • Two-phase occlusion. The single-phase test against last frame's depth is done (above); drawing last frame's visible clusters first, rebuilding the pyramid and testing the rest would remove its one-frame lag at silhouette edges, but needs the opaque pass split in two.
  • Attributes. Normals, UVs, tangents and vertex colours are carried; one UV set only. The bytes changed with each attribute (now version 5): older files are refused and must be rebuilt.
  • Seam-heavy meshes. Every UV seam is a locked boundary, so atlases with many islands reduce less.
  • Grouping. Groups are neighbours on a Morton curve, not an adjacency graph, so a level removes about half of the triangles on compact meshes and less on thin or branching ones; open meshes stop where the locked boundary pins everything.
  • Streaming and the packer. No page-in/out, and no .micromesh section in .caf or caf-pack command yet.
  • Scale. Measured on meshes up to 82 k triangles; nothing larger.
